## Exercise: `process_query`

This function is the heart of the pre-MCP chatbot: it sends the query with tool definitions, and chains multi-turn state through `previous_response_id`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Show solution

```python
def process_query(query: str = None, previous_response_id: str = None):

    ### START CODE HERE ###

    messages = [
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": (
                "You are a research assistant. "
                "Use the search_papers tool to search arXiv for academic papers "
                "on a given topic. "
                "Use the extract_info tool to get information on papers retrieved "
                "through the search_papers tool."
            )
        },
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": query
        }
    ]

    # Only pass previous_response_id when it exists (never on the first turn)
    kwargs = {}
    if previous_response_id:
        kwargs["previous_response_id"] = previous_response_id

    response = create_response(
        model="gpt-4o-mini",
        tools=tools,
        input=messages,
        **kwargs
    )

    # List all the function calls from the response object
    function_calls = [
        item for item in response.output
        if item.type == "function_call"
    ]

    # Return output text and response id if no function calls found
    if not function_calls:
        return response.output_text, response.id

    ### END CODE HERE ###
```

Three things to get right. The system prompt must name both tools and their relationship (`extract_info` operates on results from `search_papers`). The `kwargs` dance exists because the Responses API rejects a null `previous_response_id`, so it is only included when a previous turn exists — this is what gives the chatbot memory across turns. And the return must be the tuple `(response.output_text, response.id)` so the caller can pass the id back on the next turn.
:::

## Why this leads to MCP

Notice that `tools` and `TOOL_MAPPING` are hard-coded into this chatbot. Lesson 2 moves those tools into a standalone MCP server, and Lesson 3 rebuilds this same chatbot as an MCP client that discovers tools at runtime instead of hard-coding them.
